summary: Describes how a host can detect DNS64 and learn the IPv6 prefix used for address synthesis, using the well-known name ipv4only.arpa. Learning this lets nodes synthesize addresses locally and possibly avoid NAT64 on dual-stack and multi-interface deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: A device asks a special question to find out whether a translator is helping, and which code the translator adds.

questions: how to discover the nat64 prefix
how does a host detect dns64
subtitle: How an IPv6-only host asks one well-known DNS name to learn which prefix its network uses to reach IPv4.

tldr.problem: Hosts on IPv6-only networks that use NAT64 and DNS64 sometimes need to build IPv6 addresses for IPv4 peers themselves, for example when an application is handed an IPv4 address literal or when the host runs a DNSSEC-validating resolver. To do that they must know which IPv6 prefix the network uses for translation.
tldr.mechanism: The host sends a AAAA query for the well-known IPv4-only name ipv4only.arpa. and looks for the well-known IPv4 addresses 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171 inside the synthesized IPv6 addresses that come back. Whatever surrounds them is the prefix, called Pref64::/n.
tldr.outcome: A host that learns the prefix can synthesize addresses locally, and one that sees no synthesis can prefer IPv4 or another interface. The RFC calls this a best-effort transition tool and says a day will come when it is no longer needed. It has been updated by RFC 8880.

facts.label: Rediscovery
facts.value: Ten seconds before the synthetic record's TTL expires

today: RFC 7050 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8880. It has not been obsoleted. Its own exit strategy says a day will come when the tool is no longer needed, and that a node should have a configuration knob to disable prefix discovery.

sections.title: Why Hosts Need the Translation Prefix
sections.content:
Some access networks give IPv6-only nodes IPv4 connectivity with NAT64 and DNS64. DNS64 creates local IPv6 addresses for peers that only have IPv4 addresses, so a node that uses DNS can reach them. The prefix used for this is called Pref64::/n. It may be a Network-Specific Prefix (NSP) or the Well-Known Prefix (WKP).

DNS64 cannot help every case. It does not serve applications that never use DNS, such as one handed an IPv4 address literal. It also cannot synthesize addresses for nodes running a validating DNSSEC resolver, so those nodes must do the synthesis themselves. For that they have to learn the prefix.

This RFC describes a best-effort method for learning it. The synthesis procedure itself is out of scope. Knowing that synthesis happens is also useful on dual-stack or multi-interface nodes, which may then prefer IPv4 or another interface to avoid a protocol translator. The RFC adds that this will not be as robust, secure and well-behaved as an all-IPv6 system, so upgrading destinations to IPv6 is highly recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices speak only the new language and need a translator to talk to old-language friends. To write the translator's address themselves, they first have to learn which prefix the translator uses.

sections.title: How a Node Finds the Prefix
sections.content:
A node that wants to know whether NAT64 is present, and which prefixes it uses, SHALL send a DNS query for AAAA records of the Well-Known IPv4-only Name, ipv4only.arpa.. It may do so on IPv6-only and dual-stack networks. The query must have the Checking Disabled (CD) bit set to zero, otherwise the DNS64 server will not synthesize and the prefix would not be revealed.

The name has only A records, with the two Well-Known IPv4 Addresses 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171. If the reply contains AAAA records, the network is using synthesis. The node must look through all of them. It searches each IPv6 address, on octet boundaries, for a well-known IPv4 address at the locations RFC 6052 allows. If the same 32-bit value shows up more than once in one address, it repeats the search with the other well-known address. What remains around the match is the prefix. It may be the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 or a Network-Specific Prefix.

With one prefix, the node uses it both for local synthesis and for recognizing synthesis by the DNS64 server. With several, it should use all of them to recognize synthetic addresses, and it must use all of them, in the order received, when synthesizing. If the well-known addresses are not found in a standard location, the heuristic has failed.

If the AAAA query gets no positive reply, the node may send an A query for the name. A positive answer shows that the resolver is not a DNS64 server. A negative response or a timeout means no DNS64 is available, the query was filtered, or something went wrong. On timeout the node should retransmit. On a negative response it must obey the TTL before asking again. A node should only run discovery when needed, must cache the replies, and should repeat discovery ten seconds before the TTL of the synthetic AAAA record expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks about a made-up name that has only old-style addresses. The translator's reply wraps those old addresses in its own code, and the device peels the old address off to see the code.

sections.title: Validating the Discovered Prefix
sections.content:
If the channel to the DNS64 server is insecure, or the server is not trusted, an attacker can influence discovery. That could lead to denial of service, redirection or man-in-the-middle attacks. A node therefore SHOULD talk to a trusted DNS64 server over a secure channel or use DNSSEC, and NAT64 operators SHOULD provide facilities for validating discovery.

For DNSSEC validation, the operator gives each NAT64 translator a fully qualified domain name (a NAT64 FQDN) with AAAA records for Pref64::WKA. Each such address has a PTR record pointing back at the FQDN, and the records are signed. The node then follows a chain: find candidates with the AAAA query, send a PTR query for each Pref64::WKA address, compare the returned domains with its list of trusted domains, query AAAA for the chosen NAT64 FQDN, check that the answer contains the addresses seen in the first step, and validate the response with DNSSEC. If the node has no trust for the domain, the remaining steps must not be performed.

The RFC is clear about limits. DNSSEC only proves the prefix belongs to a domain used by the NAT64 FQDN. It does not prove that the node is on the network where the prefix is meant to be used, and it cannot be used in the case of a WKP.
sections.plainLanguage: To be sure the translator is honest, the device asks for its name tag, checks the tag against a list of friends it trusts, and checks that the signed record says the same thing.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks and Alternative Names
sections.content:
After learning a prefix, a node SHOULD check that it works. The prefix could be non-functional because discovery misbehaved, the IPv6 path to the NAT64 is down, the NAT64 is down, or the IPv4 path beyond it is down. A node can run a dedicated check or simply try to use the prefix, and each approach has trade-offs such as extra traffic or user-noticeable delay.

The node should use an implementation-specific check server. Failing that, it may query PTR for the Pref64::WKA address to get a NAT64 FQDN and then query A records for that name, which point to check servers run by the operator. This approach works only with NSPs, not with the WKP. The check protocol for those servers is ICMPv6: the node sends an Echo Request to the server's address synthesized with the prefix, and sends further Echo Requests one second and then two seconds later if there is no reply. With no response after three transmissions, the prefix might not be working, and the node may pick another prefix, alert the user, or proceed anyway.

Clients must not send a connectivity check to an address returned by the ipv4only.arpa. query. No server is operated there, so a check would leak to the Internet and give a false negative. Applications, operating systems, devices or networks may also run their own name, such as ipv4only.example.com, with otherwise the same steps.
sections.plainLanguage: After getting the code, the device sends a tiny test message to see if the translator really passes it along. It tries up to three times before it gives up.

sections.title: Guidance for Operators
sections.content:
The authoritative server for the well-known name SHALL use a DNS record TTL of at least 60 minutes to help caching, and the zone must be signed with DNSSEC. The exact TTL is to be tuned from operational experience.

A DNS64 operator can guide nodes by choosing how many synthetic AAAA records to return. To make nodes use several prefixes, return several records. There is no guarantee which prefix a node will end up using. To steer nodes to one prefix, or rotate prefixes for load balancing, the only guaranteed method is to return a single synthetic record with a TTL that makes the node rediscover when needed. DNS64 servers MUST NOT otherwise interfere with queries for the well-known name.

The method cannot learn rules that map specific IPv4 ranges to different prefixes, so a node uses one prefix for every IPv4 address. The RFC suggests giving servers in special ranges signed AAAA records so nodes need not synthesize, or having a router send packets to the correct NAT64.
sections.plainLanguage: The people running the translator decide how many codes to hand out and how long a code stays good. Handing out just one is the surest way to make everyone use the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The risks follow those of RFC 6147. If an attacker alters the prefix used by a DNS64 server or a node, the node's traffic goes to an altered destination. The RFC lists three outcomes: denial of service if the resulting addresses are unassigned, a flooding attack if they belong to devices that do not want the traffic, or eavesdropping if the altered NSP is routed through the attacker. DNSSEC cannot validate answers from a DNS64 server the node has no trust relationship with.

DNSSEC protection is required for AAAA queries on the well-known name, so the zone serving it has to be signed. For validation, the access network SHOULD sign the NAT64 FQDN and nodes SHOULD use the algorithm from Section 3.1.

The RFC warns against asking users to add an untrusted domain: history shows average users answer yes without thinking, so unless trusted domains can be added reliably, it is better to fail the discovery. The best mitigation is adding IPv6 support to destinations so less local synthesis is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster hands out a fake code, your messages could go to the wrong place. Signing the records and trusting only known names helps, and so does having real new-language addresses everywhere.

sections.title: The ipv4only.arpa Name and Addresses
sections.content:
IANA delegated a new second-level domain in the .ARPA zone for ipv4only.arpa., with no further delegation below it. The zone has an apex A record set with two addresses, 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171. Both are recorded in the IPv4 Special Purpose Address Registry under the name NAT64/DNS64 Discovery, allocated February 2013, with Source, Destination, Forwardable and Global set to False and Reserved-by-protocol set to True.

Appendix B explains why two addresses were wanted. The addresses cannot be non-global ones from RFC 5735, or DNS64 servers might not synthesize when the well-known prefix is used. At least two addresses help the heuristic when the bit pattern of one address appears more than once in the synthetic IPv6 address. The IAB approved the delegation but takes no architectural or technical position on the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The special made-up name lives in a reserved corner of the naming system, and two special old-style addresses were set aside so the trick works even when a code looks a bit like an address.
